title: SRE documentation: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, runbooks, and operational tooling
author: Ari Chen
content:
Summary

This page is the canonical SRE documentation bundle for Redwood Inference SLOs, error-budget policy, capacity planning guidance, standard incident review requirements, operational tooling inventory, and canonical runbook patterns. It is intended for engineering leads, SREs, on-call responders, and product owners who operate inference services (hosted API, dedicated pools, private deployments).

Goals
- Provide clear, actionable SLO definitions and error-budget handling steps.
- Standardize capacity planning calculations for GPU pools and autoscaling.
- Define incident review standards and postmortem expectations.
- Document operational tooling and recommended dashboards/alerts.
- Provide runbook templates for the most frequent classes of failures.

1) SLO definitions and rationale

Primary measurement surfaces
- Availability (successful request rate by route/model).
- Latency (p50/p95/p99 per route, measured server-side without client network tail).
- Correctness/quality (synthetic prompt set pass rate; used for regression detection not SLO).
- Throughput (requests/sec, tokens/sec for model pool).

Canonical SLOs (applies to Redwood-hosted public API; Dedicated/private may have custom SLOs negotiated in contract):
- Control plane API: availability 99.95% monthly (error budget = 0.05% of monthly minutes ~ 21.6 minutes for a 30-day month).
- Generation (text) endpoints (default tier): p95 latency < 300 ms, p99 latency < 1s measured end-to-end server-side (excludes customer network). Availability 99.9% monthly.
- Embeddings endpoints: p95 < 150ms, p99 < 500ms, availability 99.9%.
- Dedicated customer pools: availability target 99.95% (per contract), latency targets negotiated per model.

Why these numbers
- Latency SLOs reflect the cost/latency tradeoffs typical for interactive experiences; p99 objective ensures predictable worst-case.
- Availability SLOs balance operational cost with product promises; higher-tier customers receive tighter SLOs in contracts.

SLO measurement window and burn calculation
- Window: 30-day rolling window for monthly SLOs; 7-day for short-term monitoring.
- Error budget = (1 - SLO) * window duration (in minutes). Keep both absolute minutes and percent in dashboards.
- Example: 99.95% monthly availability -> allowed downtime = 0.05% of 43200 minutes = 21.6 minutes.

Error budget policy (standard escalation)
- Normal: burn rate <=1x (no action required beyond routine monitoring).
- Elevated: 1x < burn rate <= 2x for >= 24h -> notify product owner and SRE lead; evaluate mitigations.
- Urgent: burn rate >2x -> convene incident response, apply mitigations (scale pools, enable fallback models), pause non-essential rollouts.
- Critical: burn rate >4x -> immediate rollback of risky changes, enable degraded-mode routing to dedicated/legacy model variants, inform executive stakeholders.

Measurement sources and owners
- Metrics: Prometheus (service metrics), Mimir/Thanos for long-term; histograms for latency. Owner: eng-platform.
- Logging/traces: Loki + Jaeger/Honeycomb for traces. Owner: eng-observability.
- Synthetic checks: Synthetic harness (applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness) runs per minute across regions; owner: applied-ml.

2) Capacity planning guidance (GPU pools and control plane)

Inputs required for capacity plan
- Peak observed QPS (requests/sec) per route and per model.
- Average tokens generated per request and tokens/sec throughput per GPU for model variant.
- Safety headroom factor (recommended 1.5x peak for autoscaled pools, 2.0x for reserved capacity).
- Target latency percentile and buffer for autoscaling warm-up.

Sizing formula (GPU pool)
- requests_per_gpu = (tokens_per_gpu_per_sec) / (avg_tokens_per_request) * concurrency_efficiency
- required_gpus = ceil((peak_qps * headroom_factor) / requests_per_gpu)

Example calculation
- Model throughput (A100 mixed-precision): 400 tokens/sec (batching optimized).
- Avg tokens per request: 200 tokens -> requests_per_gpu = 400 / 200 = 2 req/sec.
- Peak_qps = 200 req/sec, headroom_factor = 1.5 -> required_gpus = ceil((200 * 1.5) / 2) = ceil(300/2) = 150 GPUs.
- Note: real deployments should use measured tokens/sec per model profile and account for KV-cache hit-rate which increases effective throughput.

Autoscaling policy guidance
- Warm pools: keep a small warm pool (e.g., 10% of capacity) for low-latency cold-start avoidance.
- Scale-up threshold: CPU/GPU utilization sustained >70% for 90s OR queue length > configured threshold.
- Scale-down: utilization <35% for 10m with graceful drain and traffic shifting.
- Max scaling step: avoid >2x capacity change per minute to prevent oscillation.

Control plane capacity (API servers)
- Provision based on p95 latency targets and 99.99% availability target for control plane heartbeats. Use autoscale with a minimum of 3 instances per region behind LB.

Load testing and validation checklist
1. Run synthetic traffic at 1x/1.5x/2x expected peak for at least 1 hour each.
2. Validate p95/p99 latency and success rate against SLOs.
3. Validate autoscaler behavior (scale up/down) with step traffic tests.
4. Test draining and instance replacement with live traffic.
5. Document results and expected headroom in the capacity plan artifact.

3) Reliability initiatives and prioritization

Initiative framework
- Initiatives are prioritized against potential SLO impact, user-visible incidents avoided, and engineering effort. Use a simple ROI rubric: (SLO minutes saved per month) / (engineering person-weeks).

Typical high-impact initiatives
- KV-cache prefix caching for hot prompts (reduces tokens/sec required by up to 30%).
- Model variant fallbacks and automatic routing to quantized variants under load.
- Improved batching logic in serving runtime to reduce p99 latency.
- Regional redundancy and cross-region failover tests.

Tracking and ownership
- Each initiative must have: owner, acceptance criteria, rollout plan, rollback plan, and post-rollout SLO measurement window. Track in eng-platform roadmap and link to product OKRs.

4) Incident review standards (postmortem requirements)

Overview
- All Sev2+ incidents require a postmortem within 72 hours and a final, blameless report within 7 calendar days.

Postmortem structure (required sections)
- Title and incident ID
- Severity and timeline (UTC timestamps)
- Impact summary (who/how many customers, routes affected, duration, SLO impact with minutes consumed of error budget)
- Root cause (technical sequence of events)
- Contributing factors (missing observability, cascade failures, capacity limits, release coupling, test gaps)
- Corrective actions (short-term mitigations and long-term fixes) with named owners and due dates
- Detection and response timeline (detection source, pager times, actions taken)
- Lessons learned and followups (link to related code PRs, dashboards, tests)

Review process
1. Draft postmortem filed in confluence under eng-sre/postmortems and linked to incident ticket.
2. Triage meeting within 72h with SRE lead, service owner, and product owner.
3. Publish final postmortem after reviewers sign off.
4. Track action items until completion in the reliability initiatives tracker.

Blamelessness and culture
- Emphasize systems and process failures over individual errors. Focus on reproducible mitigations and checkpoints to avoid recurrence.

5) Operational tooling: inventory and standard dashboards

Required tools (core stack)
- Metrics: Prometheus + remote-write to Thanos/Mimir for retention.
- Logs: Loki (indexed logs) + S3/GCS archive.
- Traces: Jaeger / Honeycomb for high-cardinality traces.
- Dashboards: Grafana (service / team / executive dashboards).
- Alerting/Oncall: PagerDuty (primary), Opsgenie integration for certain enterprise customers.
- Incident comms: StatusPage + internal Slack #incidents channel.
- Synthetic testing: internal synthetic harness (applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness).

Recommended dashboards (must exist for each public-facing service)
- SRE Summary board: SLO burn, error budget remaining, top alerts, active incidents.
- Latency heatmap: p50/p95/p99 across routes and regions.
- Capacity board: GPU utilization, queue length, autoscaler events, instance health.
- Dependences map: upstream model fetch times, third-party API latencies, network egress metrics.

Alerting standards
- Alert fatigue policy: only pages when actionable. Every alert must include
  - symptom description
  - one-sentence remediation steps
  - pager severity and oncall runbook link
- Threshold guidance examples:
  - High latency (p95 > SLO threshold + 20%) sustained for 2 minutes -> P1 page.
  - CPU/GPU utilization > 90% sustained 3 minutes -> P1 page.
  - Queue length > 5x baseline and growing -> P1 page.
  - Error rate > SLO window allowed rate -> P1 page.

6) Runbooks (templates and examples)

Runbook structure (required fields)
- Symptom (how this will be seen in dashboards/alerts)
- Impact (what customers/traffic are affected)
- Immediate mitigation steps (ordered, idempotent where possible)
- Diagnostic commands (CLI, Cloud console links)
- Escalation path and owners
- Recovery validation checks
- Post-incident next steps (RCA link, action items)

Example runbook: High generation p99 latency (text-generation service)
- Symptom:
  - Grafana alert: generation_service.p99_latency > 1s for 3m in region us-west-2
  - Increased queue length and GPU utilization at >85%
- Impact:
  - Interactive API requests will experience delayed responses; embeddings unaffected.
- Immediate mitigation steps:
  1. Verify alert with Grafana and check synthetic harness for region-specific failures.
  2. If autoscaler not scaling: check autoscaler logs (kubectl -n inference logs deploy/auto-scale-controller).
  3. Scale GPU pool manually: run infra CLI -> infra scale gput-pool --region us-west-2 --count +20 (replace with exact command for on-call tooling).
  4. Enable fallback routing to quantized-variant: curl -X POST $CONTROLPLANE/api/v1/route/fallback -d '{"service":"generation","variant":"quantized-v1"}' 
  5. If above fails, reduce batch size via runtime config: kubectl -n inference set env deploy/serving-runtime BATCH_MAX=8
- Diagnostic commands:
  - kubectl -n inference get pods -o wide
  - kubectl -n inference logs deploy/serving-runtime | tail -n 200
  - prometheus query: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))
  - check synthetic: curl https://synthetic.internal/redwood/health?region=us-west-2
- Escalation:
  - If manual scaling and fallback did not reduce p99 within 10 minutes: page SRE Lead (pager) and Eng-Platform oncall.
- Recovery validation:
  - Confirm p99 < SLO target for 15 minutes and queue length returning to baseline.
- Post-incident:
  - File postmortem, tag owners for action items (capacity increase, runtime tuning, batching improvement).

Example runbook: Control plane auth errors causing 5xx responses
- Symptom: sudden spike in 5xx in control-plane-auth endpoint, synthetic auth checks failing.
- Mitigation:
  1. Identify recent deploys: check deployment audit log and rollback if a control-plane change occurred in last 15 minutes.
  2. Rotate auth cache: curl -X POST $CONTROLPLANE/internal/clear-auth-cache
  3. If external KMS integration is failing, failover to cached keys (see KMS runbook) and page security.

Runbook checklist for authors
- Keep steps idempotent and short.
- Include example CLI commands and links to dashboards.
- Validate runbook annually or after any incident that exercised it.

7) Ownership and governance

- SLO steward: Eng-Platform (primary) \u2014 responsible for SLO definitions, dashboards, error-budget tracking.
- Oncall SRE: Eng-SRE \u2014 responsible for pager handling, runbook maintenance, incident response.
- Model owners (applied-ml teams): responsible for quality/regression monitoring and synthetic checks.
- Product owners: receive error-budget alerts and approve mitigations that affect product UX.

Governance process
1. Any proposed change to SLO numbers or error-budget policy must be submitted as an ADR (architecture-and-standards/api-standards) and reviewed by SRE, Product, and Legal if customer-facing.
2. Quarterly SLO review: owners must publish SLO burn trends and suggested changes.

Appendices

A. Quick reference: SLO and alert thresholds
- Control plane availability: 99.95% (allowed monthly downtime ~21.6 minutes)
- Public generation: availability 99.9%; p95 < 300ms; p99 < 1s
- Embeddings: p95 < 150ms; p99 < 500ms
- High-latency page conditions: p95 > threshold + 20% for 2m -> page P1

B. Capacity planning quick formula
- required_gpus = ceil((peak_qps * headroom_factor) / (tokens_per_gpu_per_sec / avg_tokens_per_request))

C. Useful links
- Synthetic harness runbook: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness
- Incident postmortem template: /confluence/eng-sre/postmortem-template
- Grafana SRE summary dashboard: grafana.internal/d/reds/sre-summary
- PagerDuty escalation policies: internal/pagerduty/policies
